items.note: Story 1: Association organized 1889 at Larrow Green, Gideon Vose first president, creamery built 1891.
Story 1 gives Article VII as payment by butterfat test rather than milk weight; the 'test of the station where he delivers governs' clause is absent, but the core rule is stated.

Section A says only 'the mechanism that made everything that follows possible'; never states that the rule is what made a wrong test cost money. The explicit version appears only at B3, which cannot travel into A.
Within Section A only Sill (buttermaker) and Teague (bookkeeper) appear, with no dates; Loomis as secretary/minute-book keeper appears only in Section E.
Section A never states Selby Vose was Gideon's son or manager from 1913; B3 leaves paternity open, and B does not credit A.
The station-gain ledger line appears only in Sections D and F, never inside the eight reconstructions.
Story 1: skimming station, seven miles up-valley, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896, glassware borrowed from Larrow Green.
No description in Section A of the weighing, composite sample, fixed pipette charge and percent-graduated neck; the mechanism is described only in Section F.
Story 1: Ammon & Sons of Tarnet, invoice 14 April 1897, in service 1 May 1897, with the 1898 claims rejected.
Story 1: six dozen pipettes marked 17.6 c.c., twelve dozen bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, $77.93 with line items.
Story 4 states the deficiency was 'observed, flat, all-season' at nineteen hundredths, quoting Falke's July/winter arithmetic.
Never states that a pipette cannot be checked without a burette, nor that none existed in the county.
Story 3: Ansel Keddie 1861-1934, tester 29 seasons from the 1896 opening, dismissed 30 April 1925.
Story 7 identifies the station test book 1896-1924 in Keddie's own hand; columns and initialed corrections not given but are context.
The summary leaf is never presented: Section A never attaches 3.80 to the 1896 season or 3.61 to the change of glassware from 1898. The 3.61/3.80 pair appears only as recorded-vs-true average.
Story 5: broke 8 May, borrowed measure to 10 July, nine weeks at 3.80, fall back to 3.61, question mark in the book.
Story 3 marriage to Orra Brant, Emmet's sister; Story 2 Emmet as largest patron.
The 1919 circular over the manager's signature is given, but Keddie's 17 March 1925 statement ('tested as he was taught, cannot say why') is nowhere in Section A; both halves are bolded.
Story 3: died 21 February 1934 with the imputation of dishonesty still on him.
Story 2: Hessel Bottom, six farms, Emmet Brant's the largest.
Story 2: weigh book from 1 January 1897, two daily columns, the scales 'always agreed'.
Story 4 dates the complaints to 1902. The run never states a Hollow-vs-Green gap at all, so it keeps the point on the 1902 complaints alone under the key's own clause.
Story 4: Grigg's 1908 committee, January-February-March sampling, bog-hay finding reported as the committee's finding and later defeated.
Story 2 gives 200,000 lb on a test of 3.42; Story 8 states the tests ran low 'by that same proportion', carrying the proportionality element.
Story 2: to Roy Brant 1929, lent to Ivy Keddie 1958, to Hazel after Roy's death in 1962.
Section A never names the Alder Corners Cheese Company's location (Redlow Ridge, Vessey County) or Jerome Cudd.
Story 8: the same four Hessel Bottom haulers across sixteen summers from 1915.

REQUIRED two of four independence elements inside Section A; only the artifact ('independently kept test records', 'unrelated source') is present. The other-bench/other-equipment language sits in Section D.
Story 8: the four men's milk averaged about 3.80 at Alder Corners across sixteen seasons 1915-1930 against the station's credited 3.61.

Section A calls the Alder Corners figures 'corroborating' but never states that the same milk off the same meadow in the same months kills the hay and watering explanations; that argument is made only in Section F.
Rosalie Cudd is named but not as Jerome's daughter, and the 1958 copying of sixteen seasons for Ivy Keddie is not stated.
Strawn is named only as 'the state dairy inspector' with a notebook; the Ordell circuit and the 1907-1936 span are absent from Section A (and Section F asserts 1908).
The clean lactometer record appears only in Section F, and there dated from 1908.
Story 8: crate condemned by the state dairy inspector on 12 June 1923, wrong dates rejected.
Nothing on Strawn writing no figure and making no report beyond the condemnation.
No replacement glass ordered 28 June / acknowledged 2 July 1923, and no 1924 station average of 3.80 anywhere in Section A.
The 1923 disposition of the crate into the loft is not stated (only the 1958 finding, which is A8.3's aspect), and the notebooks' 1947 transfer to the college library is absent.
Story 7: 'The patrons petitioned in January 1925.'
Story 7: Frick's board, first session 17 March 1925, second and third in the station's own weigh room, report 4 May 1925.
Story 7: watering (Vose), theft (Teague), wet hay (1908 report), 'no cause established'.
Story 7 lists exactly the four books including the 1923 inspector's notebook.
Story 7: dismissed 30 April 1925 with no cause established, award 4 May 1925 of $3,800 'without admission'.
Section A juxtaposes $19,000 and $3,800 but never states the one-fifth relation there, and never states the award was charged to the station-gain account.
Story 8: Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, graduate student at the State Agricultural College at Farland; Vaught named as co-author of Bulletin 471.
Never states that she assembled records that had never been in the same room; the series are mentioned scattered and not as an assembly.
Story 8: February 1958, crate in the loft over the station, nine pipettes surviving.
Story 8: 9 March 1958, calibrated burette, 16.72 against marked 17.6, short 0.88 c.c., one part in twenty.
Story 8: every test from 1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923 low in that proportion, 3.61 credited against a true 3.80, 0.19-point gap.
REQUIRED all four: the 40,000,000 lb (or 1.6 M/yr with the 25-year span) is not in Section A, and the identity of the 76,000 lb with the station-gain ledger total is nowhere in the answers.
Story 8: Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, no watering and no theft, cause stated; the elapsed-year intervals are omitted but the bulletin and its clearing finding carry the item.
Granddaughter, with the great-niece report identified as the Chronicle's error.
Ivy is Duncan's daughter, Duncan is Ansel's son, sourced to Duncan and Falke's correction.
Second cousins with the full derivation through Orra and Emmet.
A08: asserts 'Orra was Emmet Brant's full sister' as resolved (Story 3, repeated in Section E) and says the generations 'leave nothing open'. Gullibility deduction applied.
Declines between son and nephew as a '2-2 split among credible insiders'. The key's answer is son (Gideon), settled by the minute book; a non-abstention item, so no deduction but no point.
States that the authority descends from the founder who wrote the by-law establishing payment by test, the mechanism that made the pipette defect costly, and links it to the 1919 accusation.

A01: verdict sentence is 'the rumor is treated as unfounded' - a decision against kinship on the strength of a family member's denial, which the key says is not a record. Gullibility deduction applied.
Correctly lays out what exists: Oram's hearsay from his mother against Duncan's flat denial, and no documentary link.
0.88/17.6 = 0.05, one part in twenty; 16.27 explicitly rejected.
76,000 lb, with the 118,000 lb cascade rejected.
$19,000 at 25c; $3,800/$19,000 = 20 percent, one fifth. Both money and fraction given.
6,840 lb credited.
76,000 lb, with both denominators named: 5.00 percent of the fat delivered, 5.26 percent of the fat credited. Avoids NT-20.
$77.93 re-added from the line items.
72 pipettes (six dozen), confirmed against the $25.20 line, and 0.88 c.c. short each.
26 years and 6 weeks in service against 25 full delivery years 1898-1922, with the part-year reason stated.
A02 abstention: 'cannot be determined precisely', neither figure documentary.
Names the measuring glass/pipette as the one variable.
Herds, pasture, season, tester and procedures held constant - more than three.
Nine weeks at 3.80, back to 3.61 the day the station's own glass returned; the six-week value is explicitly rejected.
Both halves: cause travels with the equipment and not the milk, cows, feed or tester; and the stated limit that it fixes neither mechanism nor magnitude.
Four distinct reasons, each attributed to named narrators or documents, drawn from more than three narrators.
States they rest on four different record-keepers and kinds of evidence, and names the station-gain ledger as one that would hold without the 1958 measurement.
A09: answers 'no' flatly, adopting Kyle's pole ('never asked anybody anything in forty years') as settled. Gullibility deduction applied.
Answers the literal question yes - he knew the recorded numbers ran low, which is why he sent the 1919 circular.
REQUIRED three of five: the 1919 circular, the signed annual ledger sheets carrying the station-gain line, and (Section E) the manager's start in 1913.

A03: does not decline. Concludes 'the sources indicate he never connected it to the evidence already in his own signed records, and there is no evidence he suspected the glassware before its 1923 condemnation' - a definite negative verdict built on one of the two office men. Gullibility deduction applied.
Weigh book start 1 Jan 1897 against 1898/1900, resolved on independent documentary sources (Nym, Frick's exhibit list, Duncan).
1908 sampling: 'whole of 1908' rejected against the report's own Jan-Mar text, method named as the report against its own covering letter.
Ammon & Sons 'nothing into Ordell before 1900' broken by its own reproduced 1897 invoice.
Row 15 (Vose manager 1913 over 1911) also resolved with method, but E-a is capped at 3.
Explicitly flags Rundle's footnote and the Chronicle as two narrators carrying 'eleven', broken by the measurement sheet and the 1959 report.
Explicitly flags Grigg and Kepp as two narrators carrying the identical 'two tenths' misquote of Bulletin 214, broken by the bulletin's verbatim text.

Names two sources carrying 12 July 1923 and breaks the tie for 12 June on the inspector's own notebook and photostat. Breaker is a source count rather than the 28 June replacement order, but the pair is identified and broken.
Article VII's adoption year declared undeterminable (1891/1892/1893) with the lost early minute book given as the reason, while the text of the article is treated as certain.
The short-lot question is not raised as unsettleable; the reground-mould account is repeated (hedged as the maker's conjecture) with no notice that the works records are gone.
Never asks whose measure was borrowed in 1911.
Several self-refutations named explicitly: Grigg's covering letter above his own reprinted report, Ammon's history above its own 1897 invoice, Bulletin 471's introduction against its own conclusion.

Names the 1897 crate's pipettes, 16.72 against marked 17.6, ~5 percent short, derives 0.19 as the proportional consequence, and gives both boundaries (1 May 1897, 12 June 1923) with nothing changing on the farms.
Watering named to Vose and defeated by the inspector's lactometer readings at every visit (dated from 1908 - see corruption deduction).
Theft named to Teague and defeated by the cream arriving heavy in the Association's own ledger and by the 1911 interval under the same tester.
Bog hay named to the 1908 committee and Kepp and defeated by Bulletin 214's five hundredths in winter and nothing in summer, plus Alder Corners.
A07: answers 'No.' outright - the board did not examine the glassware - on the exhibit lists alone, where the key requires declining. Gullibility deduction applied.
A05: correct abstention - Duncan's and Frick's accounts given as attributed and irreconcilable, with the verdict sentence declining to settle what he believed.
148 words, within the 150-word cap.
Only three record series are named in the summary (the farm ledger, the cheese factory's records, the 1958 burette measurement); five are required.
Clean: watering, theft and hay all appear only as suspicions held at the time and are denied; headline figures ($3,800, five percent, 26 years, 1897, 1958) are all correct.

Four of six arc elements with both ends: five percent short and the 1897 glassware (onset), 1958 explanation (close), Ansel and Ivy Keddie both named. Missing 76,000 lb/$19,000 and the 1923 condemnation date.

deductions.reason: Corruption: asserts the inspector's lactometer tests were 'made at every visit from 1908 forward' - the planted 1908 start of Strawn's Ordell circuit (F074-class item, catalogued under 'Strawn's circuit begun in 1908')
Gullibility (A08): asserts Orra Brant was Emmet's full sister as resolved, in Story 3 and again in Section E
Gullibility (A01): asserts the Vose-Keddie cousinship rumour is unfounded on the strength of Duncan Keddie's denial
Gullibility (A03): asserts the manager never connected the low tests to the evidence in his own signed records and never suspected the glassware before 1923
Gullibility (A09): asserts flatly that the bookkeeper never questioned the station-gain entries
Gullibility (A07): asserts 'No' - that the 1925 board did not examine the condemned glassware
